passage:
"Asif Bhai, can you ask Abbu for the rolling bag? The blue one with wheels." Irawati dropped onto the sofa beside her brother.
"You said rolling bags were silly."
"That was before. Now twenty-two people in my class have it. Twenty-two!"
"So? Do you like it?"
Irawati paused. "It… rolls."
Asif grinned. "Wow. Strong review."
"If everyone bought it, it must be good. Twenty-two people can't all be wrong."
"Twenty-two people can all see the same advert."
"Bhai!" She hugged her old red backpack to her chest. "I just don't want to be the only one."
"Ah," Asif said, softer. "That's the real reason, na?"
Irawati picked at the zip and didn't answer.

qa.q: How many people in Irawati's class have the rolling bag?
qa.a: Twenty-two people.

qa.q: What does Irawati's pause before saying "It… rolls" suggest?
qa.a: Irawati doesn't really love the bag itself; the number of classmates who own it is what makes it feel right.

qa.q: Asif's question "Do you like it?" was a turning point. What could Irawati decide after answering it honestly?
qa.a: Irawati could decide whether the bag is worth asking for on its own, or talk openly about the fear of being the only one with a different bag.

qa.q: How does Asif see the reason behind Irawati's request by the end?
qa.a: Asif realises it is less about the bag and more about not wanting to stand out, so the teasing turns gentle.

grounding: A girl wants the bag most of her class has, mainly because so many people own it.

passage: My name is Francis, and last term I begged for a spinning-top battle set. Everyone in Class 5 had one. At break they crashed tops in a tin tray and shouted. I didn't even like it much. The tops were loud and my fingers hurt from pulling the string. But thirty kids can't all be wrong, I thought. Ankita, who sits next to me, didn't have one either. "I'd rather draw," she said. When Mum finally bought me a set, I played for two weeks. Now it's in my cupboard. Ankita still draws. I kind of wish I'd asked myself what I liked first.

qa.q: Where did the children crash their tops at break?
qa.a: In a tin tray.

qa.q: Why did Francis want the set even though pulling the string hurt?
qa.a: Francis thought that if thirty kids all had it, it had to be good, even without really enjoying it.

qa.q: Looking back, what does Francis wish had come first, and how could that help next time?
qa.a: Francis wishes they had asked what they liked before begging; next time, Francis could try a friend's set for a while before asking for one.

qa.q: How might Ankita see the whole trend from the next seat?
qa.a: Ankita seems calm about not having one and happy drawing, so the craze probably looks like something that will pass. 🙂

grounding: A child begs for a game set because the whole class has it, not because they enjoy it.

passage: Class 4 observation, Devika, age 9. Today Devika asked if she could 'please, please' get the scented gel pens by Monday. When I asked why, she said, 'Ma'am, the whole class has them. If everyone chose them, they must be the best pens.' I asked which colour she liked. She shrugged: 'Whichever the others have.' Later I saw her borrow a friend's pen, write one line, and hand it back without much interest. I did not lecture. At circle time I asked each child to share one thing they liked that nobody else did. Devika talked about her grandfather's fountain pen for five minutes, smiling. I will mention this to her mother. — Manjula Rao, class teacher

qa.q: Which pens did Devika want by Monday?
qa.a: The scented gel pens.

qa.q: What does Devika's shrug about the colour suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Devika feels little real interest in the pens themselves; the wish comes from everyone else having them.

qa.q: What did Manjula Rao choose to do instead of lecturing, and what did it bring out?
qa.a: Manjula Rao asked each child to share something only they liked, and Devika happily talked about the grandfather's fountain pen, a liking that was truly Devika's own.

qa.q: How might Devika's mother use this note when the pens come up at home?
qa.a: Devika's mother could ask what Devika really enjoys, like the fountain pen, instead of simply buying what the class has.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a child wanting the pens the whole class has, with little liking of her own.

passage:
Wednesday

Dear Diary,
Everybody in 5C has a squishy on their bag now. A peach one, a cloud one, a strawberry with a face. Today I counted: nineteen. NINETEEN. I asked Ammi for one after school and she asked what I like about them. I said they're squishy. She waited. I said everyone has one, so they must be good, right? Nineteen people can't all be making a mistake.
Farida doesn't have one. She says they smell like an eraser and she'd rather save for the drawing book. I squeezed Mahnoor's squishy at lunch and honestly it was just okay.
But I still want one. A cloud one.
Deepika

qa.q: How many squishies did Deepika count on bags in 5C?
qa.a: She counted nineteen.

qa.q: How does Deepika seem to feel about not having a squishy yet?
qa.a: Deepika seems left out and a little envious, since nineteen classmates have one, even though Mahnoor's squishy felt just okay.

qa.q: What question could help Deepika decide whether to spend on a squishy?
qa.a: Deepika could ask what to choose if no one in 5C had one, the way Farida thinks about the drawing book.

qa.q: How might Farida feel being one of the few in 5C without a squishy?
qa.a: She seems settled in her own choice, though she might sometimes feel left out when the others compare theirs.

grounding: A child wants the class craze because so many classmates have it, even though the child finds it only okay.

passage: The weekly haat set up beside the bus stand in Shirpur every Thursday. Nikita dragged her aunt Tanuja straight past the vegetables to the stall with the light-up pens. "This one, Maushi. The one with the blinking tip." "Do you need a new pen?" Nikita counted on her fingers. "Rupa has it, Salma has it, both Patil boys, the whole back bench. The whole of Class 6 bought it last week." "And what does it write like?" Nikita paused. "Blue." Tanuja laughed. "So many people bought it," Nikita insisted. "They must know something." Tanuja picked up a pen, clicked it, and scribbled on her palm. The ink skipped. She held it out without a word.

qa.q: Where was the weekly haat set up?
qa.a: It was set up beside the bus stand in Shirpur.

qa.q: Why did Nikita insist that the pen was good?
qa.a: She was eager to have what the whole of Class 6 had and felt confident they must know something, even though she couldn't say how it wrote.

qa.q: What turning point could help Nikita choose for herself here?
qa.a: Testing the pen on Tanuja's palm showed the ink skipping, which gives Nikita a real fact to weigh against the crowd.

qa.q: What was Tanuja hoping Nikita would notice when she held out the pen without a word?
qa.a: Tanuja seemed to want Nikita to see for herself that the pen skipped, rather than being told not to buy it.

grounding: A child wants the pen the whole class bought, trusting numbers over her own judgment of it.

passage:
Monday. Two boys in Farhan's class came with shiny blue space-rocket bags. Farhan looked at them and shrugged. His old green bag was fine.
Wednesday. Now six children had rocket bags. Hrithik said, "Everyone has one. It's the best bag." Farhan looked down at his green bag. It suddenly looked babyish.
Friday. Farhan begged Ammi for a rocket bag. "Why? You love your green one," she said.
"Because everyone has it. Twelve people, Ammi! They can't all be wrong."
Ammi asked what he liked about it. Farhan thought hard. "It's… blue?" He wasn't really sure.

qa.q: How many children had rocket bags by Wednesday?
qa.a: Six children had rocket bags by Wednesday.

qa.q: Why does Farhan suddenly want the rocket bag?
qa.a: He feels left out and uneasy, because so many classmates have it that it seems it must be best, not because he likes it.

qa.q: What question from Ammi helped Farhan think?
qa.a: Asking what he liked about the bag showed Farhan he wasn't really sure, apart from everyone having it.

qa.q: How might Hrithik feel about the rocket-bag trend?
qa.a: Hrithik seems excited and sure it's the best bag, maybe enjoying being part of the group.

grounding: A child wants the bag everyone in class has, less from liking it than because so many people seem to think it's best.

passage:
You want those sneakers with the lights, beta? Everyone has them? Sit with your Ujjwal Nana. Let me tell you about the spinning tops.
When I was ten, one boy brought a red wooden top to school. By the next week, every boy had one. I had a marble set I loved, but suddenly I felt like a fool with it.
I nagged my mother for three days. "Why do you want it?" she asked. I said, "Everyone has one! Twenty boys can't be wrong!"
She bought it. I spun it for a week, then it went in a drawer. I went back to marbles with my friend Faizan, who never cared about tops at all.
The top wasn't bad. I just never wanted it. I wanted what everyone had.

qa.q: What toy did young Ujjwal love before the tops came?
qa.a: He had a marble set he loved.

qa.q: Why did young Ujjwal suddenly feel like a fool with his marbles?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and left out, because every boy had a top, and so many people seemed to prove tops were better.

qa.q: What turning point in the story showed young Ujjwal what he really wanted?
qa.a: After spinning the top for a week and putting it in a drawer, he went back to marbles, showing he had only wanted what everyone had.

qa.q: How might Faizan have seen the spinning-top craze?
qa.a: Faizan never cared about tops, so he probably felt calm and unbothered while everyone else rushed to get one.

grounding: A boy wants the spinning top every classmate has, less from liking it than from feeling so many people can't be wrong.

passage:
Every child in Dhruv's class seemed to have the new football card album. At break they traded stickers loudly. Dhruv stood at the edge.
At home he asked his sister Kalyani to help him ask Papa. "But you don't even watch football," Kalyani said.
"Everyone has it. Twenty-five kids. It must be good."
There was a problem: the album cost more than the pocket money he had left that month, and Papa had said no extra money until his birthday.
Dhruv sat on his bed feeling miserable. Kalyani sat beside him. "What would you actually do with it?"
He thought. "Trade stickers… so I can be in the circle at break."
"So it's the circle you want, not the album."
Dhruv was quiet for a long time.

qa.q: How many kids did Dhruv say had the album?
qa.a: He said twenty-five kids had it.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling as he sat on his bed?
qa.a: He felt miserable and left out, sure the album must be good because so many had it.

qa.q: What could Dhruv do instead of buying the album?
qa.a: He could find other ways to join the break-time group, like asking to watch the trading or sharing a game he enjoys.

qa.q: How does Kalyani see Dhruv's wish?
qa.a: Kalyani sees that Dhruv doesn't like football and wants to belong more than he wants the album itself.

grounding: A child wants the album everyone in class has, not from liking football but from feeling that so many people can't be wrong.

passage:
By December, nearly every girl in Class 4B at Shalini's Bengaluru school had the same purple backpack with a unicorn zip. Shalini's own blue bag was only a year old and had never torn. But every morning she counted: twelve purple bags yesterday, fourteen today.
"Amma, I need the purple one," she told Minakshi at the market.
"Do you like it?" Minakshi asked.
Shalini hesitated. The unicorn looked a bit silly. "Everyone has it. So it must be the best."
Minakshi turned the price tag over. "Tell me one thing it does better than your blue bag."
Shalini thought hard, frowning at the unicorn.

qa.q: How many purple bags did Shalini count today?
qa.a: Fourteen.

qa.q: Why does Shalini want the purple bag even though the unicorn looks silly?
qa.a: She feels left out and eager to fit in, sure that if so many girls have it, it must be the best.

qa.q: Why is Minakshi's question a good one?
qa.a: It asks Shalini to judge the bag by what it does, not by how many classmates own it.

qa.q: How might Minakshi see Shalini's reason?
qa.a: Minakshi likely sees that Shalini wants to belong more than she wants the bag itself.

grounding: Shows a child wanting the bag everyone in class has, less because she likes it than because so many people having it feels like proof.

passage:
Looking back, I'm a bit embarrassed. I'm Imran, and in Class 6 everybody was playing that football card game, the one with the shiny player cards. Yusuf had forty cards. The whole back bench traded at lunch.
I didn't even like football much; I liked drawing. But when twenty kids all want the same thing, it feels like they must know something you don't. So I saved my pocket money for three weeks and bought two packs. I traded for exactly one lunch break. Then the craze moved to marbles.
The cards are still in a shoebox under my bed. What I really wanted, I think, was to sit on that back bench.

qa.q: How many cards did Yusuf have?
qa.a: Forty cards.

qa.q: What was Imran really feeling in Class 6, looking back?
qa.a: Imran felt left out and wanted to belong, so buying the cards felt like a ticket to the back bench.

qa.q: What could Imran have asked before saving for three weeks?
qa.a: Whether Imran actually liked the game, or only wanted it because so many classmates had it.

qa.q: How might Yusuf have seen Imran joining the trades?
qa.a: Yusuf probably welcomed another trader, not knowing Imran didn't care much for football.

grounding: A child recalls wanting the card game the whole class had, not from liking it but from the feeling that so many people could not be wrong.

passage:
Class teacher's note to Shankar's parents, after the monsoon break

Shankar seemed unsettled this week. Since school reopened, about fifteen children have come with the same blue astronaut bag. On Tuesday Shankar kept his old bag under the desk instead of on the hook. On Wednesday he asked me, 'Everyone has it, so it must be the best one, no?' When I asked what he liked about it, he thought, then said, 'The zip? I don't know. Everyone has it.' His own bag is in good condition, and I told him I like the patch on it. I am writing so you know where the requests at home may be coming from. Perhaps ask him what he would like about the new bag, not just who has it.

Kishore, Class 4B

qa.q: How many children came with the blue astronaut bag?
qa.a: About fifteen children.

qa.q: Why did Shankar keep his old bag under the desk?
qa.a: He probably felt embarrassed and left out, because so many classmates had the new astronaut bag.

qa.q: What does Kishore suggest the parents try, and why might it help?
qa.a: Asking Shankar what he would like about the bag, not just who has it, so he can notice whether he wants it or just wants to match.

qa.q: How might Shankar's parents feel reading the note?
qa.a: They may feel relieved to understand where his requests are coming from and better able to talk with him calmly.

grounding: A child wants the bag everyone in class has, less from liking it than from the sense that so many cannot be wrong.

passage:
25 December

Merry Christmas! Lalremsiami came over with plum cake and showed me the farm game on her mum's phone. EVERYONE in 5C plays it. Riya, Tanmay, both Sharma twins, even Kabir, who hates games. Lalremsiami says 32 people in our class have a farm. 32! That's nearly all of us. So it has to be super fun, right? I watched her play for a while. You plant carrots and wait. And wait. Honestly it was kind of boring. But I still want it so much. If 32 people like it, maybe I just didn't get it yet? I asked Papa. He said, 'Tell me one thing you liked while you watched.' I couldn't say one. I'm still asking again tomorrow.

Devika

qa.a: 32 people in the class have a farm.

qa.q: What is Devika feeling about the farm game by the end of the entry?
qa.a: Devika feels torn: a bit bored by what was seen, yet still wanting the game badly because so many classmates play it.

qa.q: How could Papa build on his question?
qa.a: Papa could let Devika try the game a few times and then talk about whether it is actually fun, rather than how many people play it.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami see Devika's interest?
qa.a: Lalremsiami probably sees it as a chance to share a favourite game with a friend, not as pressure.

grounding: A child wants the game everyone in class plays, less from liking it than from the sense that so many people cannot all be wrong.

passage: During the week of the temple fair at Sirsi, every child in Class 3 seemed to own the same metal spinning top with a red light inside. They spun them on the school verandah at every break. Aditi's wooden top, the one Ajja had carved, stayed in her bag. 'Why don't you get the light-top?' asked Charu. 'Everyone has it.' That evening at the fair, Aditi tugged Amma's sari at the toy stall. 'That one. Please. Everyone has it.' Amma held it out to her. 'What do you like about it?' Aditi frowned. It was heavy. The light hurt her eyes a little. 'Everyone...' she began, then stopped. 'So many kids can't be wrong, na?' Amma waited. Aditi looked down at her bag, where the wooden top was.

qa.q: Who had carved Aditi's wooden top?
qa.a: Ajja had carved it.

qa.q: Why did Aditi stop in the middle of saying 'Everyone...'?
qa.a: Aditi felt unsure and a little confused, noticing she didn't actually like the heavy top and had wanted it mainly because everyone had one.

qa.q: What did Amma do that helped Aditi think?
qa.a: Amma asked what she liked about the top and then waited, giving Aditi space to notice her real reasons.

qa.q: How might Charu see Aditi's wooden top?
qa.a: Charu seems to see it as odd or out of date, simply because it is different from what everyone else has.

grounding: A child wants the spinning top everyone has, less because she likes it than because so many children seem to.

passage: In the New Year holidays in Kyoto, Hiroshi went shopping with his mother for the new school term. At the stationery shop, he pointed at the blue robot pencil case. "That one." "You liked the green one last week," his mother said. "Everyone in my class has the robot one. Tariq has it. Even the teacher said it's nice." "Do you like it?" Hiroshi hesitated. The robot's eyes were a bit strange. But twenty-six people couldn't all be wrong about it. "Yes," he said. His mother bought it. At home, he put it next to his old green one and looked at them for a while. He wasn't sure which he liked. He only knew which one everyone had.

qa.q: Who in Hiroshi's class has the robot pencil case?
qa.a: Tariq has it, and everyone in his class.

qa.q: Why did Hiroshi hesitate when his mother asked if he liked it?
qa.a: He felt unsure, because he thought the robot's eyes were a bit strange but wanted what everyone else had.

qa.q: What question could help Hiroshi choose next time?
qa.a: He could ask himself which one he would pick if nobody in class had either, to find his own preference.

qa.q: How does Hiroshi's mother see his choice?
qa.a: She seems doubtful, remembering he liked the green one and asking whether he really likes the robot case.

grounding: Shows a child wanting the pencil case everyone in class has, less from liking it than from the sense that so many can't be wrong.
